Commission policy automatically to extend zone limits as the base municipality annexes more land. Consequently, the Commission's concern with demography and population movement to the suburbs is largely misplaced, because there is no concomitant contraction of zone size as a base municipality's population decreases and there is an automatic zone expansion as municipal boundaries expand.
The Committee criticizes the weight accorded three economic studies in the Interim Report, namely, the Pennjerdel, Freight ForwardersInstitute, and Department of Transportation studies. These studies focused primarily on large cities and dealt mainly with demographic and industrial location information. It is further asserted that a close look at these studies reveals the inherent contradictions in across-the-board expansion and the need for individual determination.
The Committee points out that the commercial zone exemption is predicated on the existence of economic interaction between the base municipality and its surrounding area. The population-mileage formula was developed in the mid-1940's to effectuate the exemption by reflecting the extent of this economic interaction. It is the Committee's thesis that there has been a change in the degree of city and suburban mutual interaction. Today, metropolitan areas are decentralized, and outlying suburban communities are self-sufficient. There is little interaction between these communities and the center city. The contemporary urban model is best described by the "multi-nucleated concept" - a concept which holds that the urban place no longer has a single node but is rather comprised of a series of nodes scattered over a much larger area.
